An Assortment of Problems in Permutation Patterns: Unimodality, Equivalence, Derangements, and Sorting

Vincent Vatter ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, University of Florida, Gainesville, Florida, USA.
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We collect open problems in permutation patterns on four themes: rank-unimodality in the permutation pattern poset, Wilf-equivalence and shape-Wilf-equivalence, the enumeration of derangements in permutation classes, and sorting by stacks in series, generalized stacks, and restricted containers (𝒞\mathcal{C}-machines).

1. Introduction

This paper accompanies a talk I gave at the pre-conference workshop for early career researchers at Permutation Patterns 2025, the 23rd year of the conference series, held at the University of St Andrews and organized by Christian Bean and Ruth Hoffmann. It is not a list of the best-known or most difficult open problems in permutation patterns, but simply an assortment of problems on a few themes: problems I have encountered, wondered about, or been asked about. Many are of the “someone really ought to…” variety. A few are folklore, and some may be trivial. This is not meant as a roadmap for the field; describing what I feel are the deepest or most important open problems would require a different approach and considerably more buildup. Think of this instead as a collection of interesting attractions that do not take too long to reach.

The best-known open problem in the field is surely the enumeration of 13241324-avoiding permutations. This one is easy to reach, but many have looked and progress has been hard to come by. Asked why, Zeilberger replied, “Because life is hard. The few combinatorial objects that we can count exactly are the trivial ones” [57] (emphasis in original). There are, in any case, plenty of places to read more about this conundrum [60, 32, 21, 48, 22, 33, 14, 34, 15]. We have nothing new to add about this problem, and so turn to areas that seem more tractable, or at least where we have less evidence of intractability.

The primary venue for results in permutation patterns, and for the exchange of open problems, has been the Permutation Patterns conference series, founded in 2003 by Michael Albert and Michael Atkinson at the University of Otago in Dunedin, New Zealand. Atkinson, who introduced Albert to the subject [58], drew many of the field’s current researchers into permutation patterns; his retirement was honored at Permutation Patterns 2013. Albert and Atkinson, and the conference series they founded, have shaped the research agenda considerably, and the conference’s tradition of open problems sessions has been particularly influential. For his part, Albert became a central figure in permutation patterns, known for his computational and collaborative approach to the subject, and retired in 2024. In this spirit, many of the problems here beg for computation, either because data is the goal, or just to better illuminate the path forward.

There are earlier collections of open problems that the reader may also find valuable. Wilf, widely regarded as a founder of the field and the plenary speaker at the inaugural Permutation Patterns conference in 2003, wrote a survey in 1999 [89] at an early stage in its development; I particularly enjoyed reading it as a graduate student. In that survey, Wilf expressed doubt about the Stanley–Wilf conjecture due to recent results of Alon and Friedgut [3]; his doubt was proved wrong a few years later when Marcus and Tardos [59] proved it. Wilf also recounted Stanley’s skepticism about the Noonan–Zeilberger conjecture [63] that every finitely based permutation class has a D-finite generating function; that skepticism was vindicated many years later when Garrabrant and Pak [43] disproved the conjecture.

Another valuable resource is Steingrímsson’s 2013 survey [80], which covers a broad range of topics, including the Möbius function of the permutation pattern poset, topological properties of intervals, vincular and mesh patterns, and the structure of growth rates. Steingrímsson is himself a leader in the field who has trained many of its current researchers; he delivered the plenary address at Permutation Patterns 2009.

For readers seeking broader introductions to permutation patterns, several general references are available. Kitaev’s Patterns in Permutations and Words [50] is a comprehensive compendium of the field. Bóna’s undergraduate textbook A Walk Through Combinatorics [23] contains a very accessible introduction to the area, while his monograph Combinatorics of Permutations [24] treats the subject in greater depth. Finally, I can’t help but recommend my own survey [85] that appears in the Handbook of Enumerative Combinatorics.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 concerns rank-unimodality of intervals in the permutation pattern poset. Section 3 discusses symmetries and Wilf-equivalence. Section 4 addresses the enumeration of derangements in permutation classes. Section 5 looks at sorting machines. Below, we collect the basic definitions and offer some remarks on permutations as relational structures.

Basic definitions

The basic notions of permutation patterns are easily stated. With apologies to those who view permutations as elements of a Coxeter group (Tenner [83]), we use the term length to mean the number of entries in a permutation, which we denote by |π||\pi|. We identify a permutation π\pi with its plot: the set of points {(i,π⁡(i))}\{(i,\pi(i))\} in the plane. When we speak of an entry being to the left or right of, or above or below, another entry, we refer to their relative positions in the plot. Similarly, an entry lies to the southeast of another if it is both to the right and below, and so on for the other cardinal directions.

A permutation σ\sigma is contained in π\pi, written σ≤π\sigma\leq\pi, if π\pi has a subsequence that is order-isomorphic to σ\sigma, meaning its entries appear in the same relative order; otherwise π\pi avoids σ\sigma. In terms of plots, σ≤π\sigma\leq\pi means that some selection of points from the plot of π\pi, when rescaled, yields the plot of σ\sigma. Figure 1 illustrates these definitions. This containment relation is a partial order, and we refer to it as the permutation pattern order.

A permutation class is a downset (or order ideal) in this poset: a set 𝒞\mathcal{C} of permutations such that if π∈𝒞\pi\in\mathcal{C} and σ≤π\sigma\leq\pi, then σ∈𝒞\sigma\in\mathcal{C}. We denote by 𝒞n\mathcal{C}_{n} the set of permutations of length nn in a class 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Every permutation class 𝒞\mathcal{C} is characterized by its basis, the set of minimal permutations not in 𝒞\mathcal{C}. We write Av⁡(B)\operatorname{Av}(B) for the class of permutations avoiding every element of BB. The basis of a class is necessarily an antichain (a set of pairwise incomparable permutations), and since the permutation pattern order contains infinite antichains, bases can be infinite.

Permutations as relational structures

The study of permutation patterns fits naturally into the broader combinatorics of relational structures. In terms of the plot, a permutation is a set of nn points equipped with two total orders: the left-to-right order (by xx-coordinate) and the bottom-to-top order (by yy-coordinate). As Cameron [28] observes, this perspective clarifies what it means for one permutation to be contained in another: containment is simply the induced substructure relation, the same notion studied in the context of graphs (induced subgraphs), posets (induced subposets), integer partitions (Young’s lattice), and other combinatorial objects.

This point of view will be relevant in the next section, where we compare unimodality results for permutations with analogous results for partitions and words. In most of those cases, the containment order is the natural one for relational structures of that type, and the questions (and answers) turn out to be surprisingly different.

2. Unimodality

We begin with what is perhaps the easiest of these problems to state, though it may well be among the hardest to prove. A finite sequence a0,a1,…,ana_{0},a_{1},\dots,a_{n} is said to be unimodal if there exists an index kk such that

a0≤a1≤⋯≤ak≥⋯≥an;a_{0}\leq a_{1}\leq\cdots\leq a_{k}\geq\cdots\geq a_{n};

that is, the sequence weakly increases to its maximum and then weakly decreases. A polynomial is said to be unimodal if its sequence of coefficients is unimodal. There are scores of unresolved unimodality questions in combinatorics and algebra; for a sample, the reader is referred to Stanley’s 1986 survey [78], many of whose conjectures remain open.

Given a permutation π\pi of length nn, let aka_{k} denote the number of permutations of length kk contained in π\pi. Is the sequence a0,a1,…,ana_{0},a_{1},\dots,a_{n} necessarily unimodal? To state this in a more refined form, we recall a few definitions. The set of all permutations contained in a given permutation π\pi forms, under the containment order, a principal downset (also called a principal order ideal). This is a ranked poset, with the rank of a permutation given by its length. A ranked poset is said to be rank-unimodal if the sequence counting the number of elements at each rank is unimodal.

Conjecture 2.1.

Every principal downset in the permutation pattern poset is rank-unimodal.

This phenomenon may have first been noted in the permutation pattern context by Murphy, who wrote at the end of his 2002 thesis [62, p. 348], emphasis added:

There exists a program that takes a permutation of arbitrary length (usually about 24) and returns the set of all permutations involved in it, sorted by length. This is a simple but somewhat expensive way of finding the basis of the closure of a given permutation or set of permutations. The nicest thing about the program is the waisted shape of the output. Here is the number of permutations of each length in one permutation of length 17:

1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 36, 87, 210, 486, 927, 1315, 1348, 1005, 549, 218, 61, 11, 1.1,\ 1,\ 2,\ 5,\ 14,\ 36,\ 87,\ 210,\ 486,\ 927,\ 1315,\ 1348,\ 1005,\ 549,\ 218,\ 61,\ 11,\ 1.

We may go further and ask whether all intervals in this poset are rank-unimodal. The interval [σ,π][\sigma,\pi] is the set of all permutations τ\tau satisfying σ≤τ≤π\sigma\leq\tau\leq\pi. It was in this generality that McNamara and Steingrímsson posed the following conjecture, which subsumes Conjecture 2.1.

Conjecture 2.2 (McNamara and Steingrímsson [61, Conjecture 9.4]).

Every interval in the permutation pattern poset is rank-unimodal.

Analogous structures

Before surveying what is known for the permutation pattern poset, we briefly consider analogous questions for other combinatorial structures. The picture that emerges is mixed: rank-unimodality holds in some settings but fails in others, which leaves the permutation case genuinely uncertain.

In the consecutive pattern poset on permutations, rank-unimodality of intervals was established by Elizalde and McNamara [39]. However, their proof relies on the particularly constrained nature of consecutive containment (every permutation covers at most two others in this order) and does not appear to shed light on the standard (not-necessarily-consecutive) permutation pattern order.

For integer partitions, the situation is murkier. The containment order on partitions is defined by μ≤λ{\mu\leq\lambda} if the Ferrers diagram of μ\mu fits inside that of λ\lambda; equivalently, if μi≤λi\mu_{i}\leq\lambda_{i} for all ii, padding with zeros as needed. This order makes the set of all partitions into a distributive lattice, called Young’s lattice. The principal downset generated by the m×nm\times n rectangular partition (m,m,…,m)(m,m,\dots,m) consisting of nn parts each equal to mm is denoted by L⁡(m,n)L(m,n), and its rank-generating function is a Gaussian polynomial. Gaussian polynomials have been known to be unimodal since the mid-nineteenth century, although a combinatorial proof was not given until O’Hara [64] in 1990, later exposited colorfully by Zeilberger [90].

One might hope that all principal downsets in Young’s lattice are rank-unimodal. Indeed, in 1986 Pouzet and Rosenberg [65, p. 367] asked something far more general: are principal downsets in the natural ordering on any type of finite relational structures rank-unimodal? This was answered in the negative only a year later by Stanton [79], who exhibited a non-unimodal principal downset in Young’s lattice. The partition (8,8,4,4)(8,8,4,4) has rank sequence

1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 11, 15, 17, 21, 23, 27, 28,31, 30, 31¯, 27, 24, 18, 14, 8, 5, 2, 1.1,\ 1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 5,\ 6,\ 9,\ 11,\ 15,\ 17,\ 21,\ 23,\ 27,\ 28,\ \underline{31,\ 30,\ 31},\ 27,\ 24,\ 18,\ 14,\ 8,\ 5,\ 2,\ 1.

Stanton’s counterexample for integer partitions also precludes any thoughts of a graph analogue of Conjecture 2.1, because it shows that the enumeration of induced subgraphs of the graph K8∪K8∪K4∪K4K_{8}\cup K_{8}\cup K_{4}\cup K_{4} is not unimodal.

Although the answer to their question was negative, Pouzet and Rosenberg [65, Corollary 2.11] did establish what might be called the “first half” of rank-unimodality: in any principal downset of a finite relational structure, the rank sequence is weakly increasing up to at least the middle rank. Combined with the symmetry of Young’s lattice, this gives another proof of the unimodality of the Gaussian polynomials. Specialized to permutations, it guarantees that the rank sequence of any principal downset in the permutation pattern poset increases up to at least half its length.

Words over a finite alphabet under the subword order are much better behaved. Chase [29] proved that principal downsets are not merely rank-unimodal but rank-log-concave, a stronger property we now define.

Log-concavity

A sequence a0,a1,…,ana_{0},a_{1},\dots,a_{n} of nonnegative terms is said to be log-concave if ak2≥ak−1​ak+1{a_{k}^{2}\geq a_{k-1}a_{k+1}} for all 1≤k≤n−1{1\leq k\leq n-1}, and a polynomial p⁡(x)=a0+a1​x+⋯+an​xnp(x)=a_{0}+a_{1}x+\cdots+a_{n}x^{n} is log-concave if its sequence of coefficients is log-concave. Log-concavity implies unimodality because it shows that the ratios ak/ak−1a_{k}/a_{k-1} are weakly decreasing, so once this ratio drops below 11, it remains below 11.

We cannot hope for log-concavity in the permutation pattern poset. The rank sequence of every nontrivial downset begins 1,1,2,…1,1,2,\dots, but 12<1⋅21^{2}<1\cdot 2 so these sequences are not log-concave. Even ignoring the empty permutation, sequences beginning 1,2,51,2,5 or 1,2,61,2,6 (both common) fail log-concavity because 22<1⋅52^{2}<1\cdot 5.

Nevertheless, log-concavity can play a key role in establishing unimodality, via the following classical result due to Ibragimov [46] and Keilson and Gerber [49].11 1 It should be remarked that the product of two unimodal polynomials is not necessarily unimodal. For example, 1+x+3​x21+x+3x^{2} is unimodal but (1+x+3​x2)2=1+2​x+7​x2+6​x3+9​x4(1+x+3x^{2})^{2}=1+2x+7x^{2}+6x^{3}+9x^{4} is not.

Proposition 2.3.

A polynomial p⁡(x)p(x) with positive coefficients is log-concave if and only if p⁡(x)​q​(x)p(x)q(x) is unimodal for every unimodal polynomial q⁡(x)q(x).

Layered permutations and compositions

One might hope that the conjecture is at least resolved for layered permutations, a particularly tractable permutation class. We briefly recall their definition.

The direct sum, or simply sum, of permutations π\pi of length mm and σ\sigma of length nn is the permutation π⊕σ\pi\oplus\sigma of length m+n{m+n} defined by

(π⊕σ)​(i)={π⁡(i)for ​1≤i≤m,σ⁡(i−m)+mfor ​m+1≤i≤m+n.(\pi\oplus\sigma)(i)\;=\;\begin{cases}\pi(i)&\text{for }1\leq i\leq m,\\ \sigma(i-m)+m&\text{for }m+1\leq i\leq m+n.\end{cases}

Visually, the plot of π⊕σ\pi\oplus\sigma places the plot of σ\sigma above and to the right of the plot of π\pi. The operation is associative, so expressions like π⊕σ⊕τ\pi\oplus\sigma\oplus\tau do not require parentheses.

A permutation is layered if it can be expressed as a sum of decreasing permutations; equivalently, the layered permutations are precisely Av⁡(231,312)\operatorname{Av}(231,312). Every layered permutation has a unique decomposition π=δ1⊕δ2⊕⋯⊕δk\pi=\delta_{1}\oplus\delta_{2}\oplus\cdots\oplus\delta_{k} where each δi\delta_{i} is a decreasing permutation, and so layered permutations are in bijection with compositions: the composition c=c(1)c(2)⋯c(k)c=c(1)c(2)\cdots c(k) corresponds to the layered permutation with consecutive decreasing layers of lengths c⁡(1)c(1), c⁡(2)c(2), …\dots, c⁡(k)c(k). For example, the composition (3,1,4)(3,1,4) corresponds to the layered permutation 321⊕1⊕4321=321 4 8765321\oplus 1\oplus 4321=321\,4\,8765.

Under this bijection, the pattern containment order on layered permutations corresponds to the (generalized) subword order on compositions. Concretely, a composition u=u(1)⋯u(k)u=u(1)\cdots u(k) with kk parts is a subword of a composition ww with ℓ\ell parts if there exist indices 1≤i1<i2<⋯<ik≤ℓ1\leq i_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{k}\leq\ell such that u⁡(j)≤w⁡(ij)u(j)\leq w(i_{j}) for all 1≤j≤k1\leq j\leq k. Thus π≤σ\pi\leq\sigma in the permutation pattern order on layered permutations if and only if the corresponding compositions satisfy u≤wu\leq w in the subword order.

Sagan [70] established unimodality for principal downsets of compositions, which might seem to settle the layered permutation case. However, there is a catch: the order Sagan considers is not the subword order.

In Sagan’s componentwise order, a composition u=u(1)⋯u(k)u=u(1)\cdots u(k) is contained in w=w(1)⋯w(ℓ)w=w(1)\cdots w(\ell) if k≤ℓk\leq\ell and u⁡(i)≤w⁡(i)u(i)\leq w(i) for all 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k. This is a natural analogue of Young’s lattice, ordering compositions by componentwise comparison of their parts. But it is not the subword order, which corresponds to the permutation pattern order on layered permutations and has been more commonly studied (see, for example, Bergeron, Bousquet-Mélou, and Dulucq [13] and Sagan and Vatter [71]).

The difference is that in the subword order, embeddings need not align initial entries. For instance, the composition (2)(2) is not contained in (1,2)(1,2) under the componentwise order, yet the corresponding layered permutations satisfy 21≤1 3221\leq 1\,32 in the permutation pattern order.

Sagan’s main result is the following. The proof is short and instructive.

Theorem 2.4 (Sagan [70, Theorem 3.3]).

The principal downset of any composition is rank-unimodal under the componentwise order.

Proof.

Let fw​(x)f_{w}(x) denote the rank-generating polynomial for the principal downset of the composition w=w(1)⋯w(ℓ)w=w(1)\cdots w(\ell) in the componentwise order. If u=u(1)⋯u(k)u=u(1)\cdots u(k) is contained in ww, then either uu is empty, or u⁡(1)≤w⁡(1)u(1)\leq w(1) and u(2)⋯u(k)≤w(2)⋯w(ℓ)u(2)\cdots u(k)\leq w(2)\cdots w(\ell). This yields the recurrence

fw(x)= 1+(x+x2+⋯+xw⁡(1))fw(2)⋯w(ℓ)(x),f_{w}(x)\;=\;1\,+\,\bigl(x+x^{2}+\cdots+x^{w(1)}\bigr)\,f_{w(2)\cdots w(\ell)}(x),

with fε​(x)=1f_{\varepsilon}(x)=1 for the empty composition.

We proceed by induction on the number of parts of ww. The base case fε​(x)=1{f_{\varepsilon}(x)=1} is trivially unimodal. For the inductive step, the polynomial x+x2+⋯+xw⁡(1)x+x^{2}+\cdots+x^{w(1)} is log-concave, so by Proposition 2.3, its product with the (inductively) unimodal polynomial fw(2)⋯w(ℓ)(x)f_{w(2)\cdots w(\ell)}(x) is unimodal. Since the coefficient of xx in this product equals 11, adding the constant term 11 preserves unimodality. ∎

Although the componentwise and subword orders are different, for compositions with weakly decreasing part sizes, the principal downsets under the two orders have the same rank sequences. To see this, observe that if w=w(1)⋯w(ℓ)w=w(1)\cdots w(\ell) is weakly decreasing, then any embedding of uu into ww in the subword order can be shifted left to produce an embedding in the componentwise order. Thus the set of compositions contained in ww is the same under both orders, even though the order relations among them may differ, and so the principal downsets of compositions with weakly decreasing parts are rank-unimodal by Sagan’s Theorem 2.4. By symmetry (reversing the compositions), the unimodality also holds when ww is weakly increasing.

Corollary 2.5.

The principal downset of a composition with monotone parts is rank-unimodal in the subword order. Hence, the principal downset of the corresponding layered permutation is rank-unimodal.

In particular, this covers the case of “rectangular” compositions (ℓ,ℓ,…,ℓ)(\ell,\ell,\dots,\ell), which was the original question the author asked Sagan about at Permutation Patterns 2007. The general case, even for layered permutations, remains open.

Conjecture 2.6.

The principal downset of every composition is rank-unimodal in the subword order. Hence, the principal downset of every layered permutation is rank-unimodal.

Albert and the author have verified this conjecture for all compositions of length 3434 or less. This is of course a special case of Conjecture 2.1, which is itself a special case of Conjecture 2.2.

3. Equivalence

The permutation pattern order has a natural symmetry group, the dihedral group D4D_{4} of order eight, visualized in Figure 2 as symmetries of the square. These symmetries act on the plots of permutations, and in the permutation patterns literature the group is commonly described as generated by three reflections: reverse π↦πr{\pi\mapsto\pi^{\mathrm{r}}} (reflection about the vertical axis), complement π↦πc{\pi\mapsto\pi^{\mathrm{c}}} (reflection about the horizontal axis), and inverse π↦π−1{\pi\mapsto\pi^{-1}} (reflection about the main diagonal). The standard presentation of dihedral groups instead uses one reflection and one rotation; here, this would be any one of the four reflections together with the 90∘90^{\circ} rotation π↦(πc)−1{\pi\mapsto(\pi^{\mathrm{c}})^{-1}} or the 270∘270^{\circ} rotation π↦(πr)−1{\pi\mapsto(\pi^{\mathrm{r}})^{-1}}. As indicated by Figure 2, composing two reflections yields a rotation, while composing three reflections yields another reflection.

These symmetries partition the permutations of each length into symmetry classes: permutations π\pi and σ\sigma lie in the same symmetry class if σ=Φ⁡(π)\sigma=\Phi(\pi) for some symmetry Φ\Phi. Since symmetries are automorphisms of the permutation pattern order, any enumerative question about π\pi-avoiding permutations is equivalent to the corresponding question about Φ⁡(π)\Phi(\pi)-avoiding permutations. (This applies only when counting all permutations, however; when we impose additional constraints, such as counting derangements in the next section, we lose symmetries.)

It can be useful to adopt a group-theoretic perspective. For permutations of length nn, let

ρ=n(n−1)⋯21=idr=idc.\rho={n(n-1)\cdots 21}=\mathrm{id}^{\mathrm{r}}=\mathrm{id}^{\mathrm{c}}.

Then complement is left multiplication by ρ\rho, πc=ρ∘π\pi^{\mathrm{c}}=\rho\circ\pi, while reverse is right multiplication by ρ\rho, πr=π∘ρ\pi^{\mathrm{r}}=\pi\circ\rho. Since ρ\rho is an involution, identities among the symmetries become straightforward calculations. For example, (πr)−1=(π∘ρ)−1=ρ−1∘π−1=ρ∘π−1=(π−1)c(\pi^{\mathrm{r}})^{-1}=(\pi\circ\rho)^{-1}=\rho^{-1}\circ\pi^{-1}=\rho\circ\pi^{-1}=(\pi^{-1})^{\mathrm{c}}.

Two permutations can have equinumerous avoidance classes without being symmetries of each other. The classical example is that both Av⁡(231)\operatorname{Av}(231) and Av⁡(321)\operatorname{Av}(321) are counted by the Catalan numbers, yet 231231 and 321321 lie in different symmetry classes. This motivated Wilf to ask, in the 1980s, for a classification of when avoiding one permutation is equally restrictive as avoiding another.22 2 Wilf never raised this question in print, but Babson and West [10] and Stanley [31, p. 357] both state that he posed it in the 1980s. We say that π\pi and σ\sigma are Wilf-equivalent, written π∼σ\pi\sim\sigma, if |Avn⁡(π)|=|Avn⁡(σ)||\operatorname{Av}_{n}(\pi)|=|\operatorname{Av}_{n}(\sigma)| for all nn. Symmetry implies Wilf-equivalence, but as the example 231∼321231\sim 321 shows, the converse does not hold.

Before discussing Wilf-equivalence further, we pause to note that while counting symmetry classes turns out to be straightforward, this was not always appreciated. In his November 1962 Scientific American column, Gardner [42] described the problem of counting “essentially different” placements of nn non-attacking rooks on an n×nn\times n chessboard (equivalent to counting symmetry classes of permutations of length nn), writing that “the task of eliminating rotation and reflection duplicates is so difficult that it is not known how many essentially different solutions exist even on as low-order a board as the 8×8{8\times 8}.” In fact, this is a routine application of Pólya theory, and moreover, Lucas had already solved the problem in his 1891 book Théorie des Nombres [56, pp. 220–222], well before Pólya.33 3 For a similar problem that is actually difficult, consider the nn-queens problem, which asks to count symmetry classes of non-attacking placements of nn queens on an n×nn\times n board. Unlike the rooks problem, there is no simple formula: the sequence of solutions (A000170) begins 1,0,0,2,10,4,40,92,352,…1,0,0,2,10,4,40,92,352,\dots, and the current record, n=27n=27, required a year-long massively parallel computation [67]. We refer to the survey of Bell and Stevens [12].

Wilf-equivalence is harder than this. If π∼σ\pi\sim\sigma, then π\pi and σ\sigma must have the same length. The permutations of lengths 11, 22, and 33 each form a single Wilf-equivalence class. For length 44, there are 77 symmetry classes but only 33 Wilf-equivalence classes; establishing that there are exactly 33 required considerable work, completed by Stankova [75] in 1996. In their 2002 paper, Stankova and West [77] extended the classification to length 77. These values are displayed in Table 1. The enumeration of Wilf-equivalence classes has remained stuck here since 2002.

Question 3.1.

How many Wilf-equivalence classes of permutations of length 88 are there?

A first step toward extending this to length 88 would be to compute |Avn⁡(β)||\operatorname{Av}_{n}(\beta)| for each β\beta of length 88 and sufficiently large nn to separate the symmetry classes into candidate Wilf-equivalence classes, then to check which apparent equivalences are already explained by known results. Perhaps existing theorems suffice, or perhaps there are new Wilf-equivalences waiting to be discovered.

Sufficient conditions: shape-Wilf-equivalence

Most known Wilf-equivalences can be explained by a stronger notion of equivalence. A full rook placement (or frp) of shape λ\lambda is a Ferrers board of shape λ\lambda with one rook in each row and column. Every permutation π\pi of length nn corresponds to the n×nn\times n square frp with rooks in positions (i,π⁡(i))(i,\pi(i)); this is simply the plot of π\pi with grid lines added. There is a natural containment order on frps: RR is contained in SS if RR can be obtained from SS by deleting rows and columns. Restricted to square frps, this coincides with the pattern order on permutations.

We say that an frp contains a permutation σ\sigma if it contains the square frp corresponding to σ\sigma, and otherwise that it avoids σ\sigma. Note that the entire square must fit within the frp; for instance, an frp whose rooks happen to form a 2121-pattern might still avoid 2121 if the top-right corner doesn’t fit inside the Ferrers board. A general frp can be visualized as a plot enclosed by a staircase boundary (a Dyck path). Permutations β\beta and γ\gamma are shape-Wilf-equivalent if, for every Ferrers shape λ\lambda, the number of β\beta-avoiding frps of shape λ\lambda equals the number of γ\gamma-avoiding frps of shape λ\lambda. Shape-Wilf-equivalence implies Wilf-equivalence (by restricting to square shapes), but is strictly stronger.

The power of shape-Wilf-equivalence comes from a closure property first observed by Babson and West [10] (implicit in the proofs of their Theorems 1.6 and 1.9) and made explicit by Backelin, West, and Xin [11, Proposition 2.3].

Proposition 3.2.

If α\alpha and β\beta are shape-Wilf-equivalent, then α⊕γ{\alpha\oplus\gamma} and β⊕γ{\beta\oplus\gamma} are shape-Wilf-equivalent for every permutation γ\gamma.

The idea is simple and illustrated in Figure 3. Given an α⊕γ\alpha\oplus\gamma-avoiding frp, consider the shadow cast by copies of γ\gamma: the cells lying southwest of every copy of γ\gamma contained in the frp (where, as always, a copy of γ\gamma means the full square frp corresponding to γ\gamma, not merely rooks forming a γ\gamma-pattern). This shadow forms a Ferrers board (shown shaded), and the rooks within it, after removing empty rows and columns, form an α\alpha-avoiding frp. We then apply whatever bijection witnesses the shape-Wilf-equivalence of α\alpha and β\beta to obtain a β\beta-avoiding frp of the same shape. Restoring the empty rows and columns and replacing the portion of the frp outside the shadow yields a β⊕γ\beta\oplus\gamma-avoiding frp of the original shape.

From one shape-Wilf-equivalence, Proposition 3.2 generates infinitely many others. In fact, only two basic shape-Wilf-equivalences are known.

Theorem 3.3 (Backelin, West, and Xin [11, Theorem 2.1]).

For every k≥1k\geq 1, the permutations k(k−1)⋯21k(k-1)\cdots 21 and 12⋯k12\cdots k are shape-Wilf-equivalent.

The case k=2k=2 was proved by West [86] and k=3k=3 by Babson and West [10]. Krattenthaler [53] gave an elegant bijective proof of the general case using Fomin’s growth diagrams. This result has since been generalized to binary matrices by de Mier [35] and to words by Jelínek and Mansour [47].

Theorem 3.4 (Stankova and West [77]).

The permutations 231231 and 312312 are shape-Wilf-equivalent.

A bijective proof was later given by Bloom and Saracino [19], and this is the bijection labeled BS in Figure 3. This bijection is wonderfully simple: they establish a correspondence between 231231-avoiding frps and labeled Dyck paths, then locally transform the labels, and finally map back to 312312-avoiding frps. Guo, Krattenthaler, and Zhang [45] have since extended Theorem 3.4 to words.

Theorem 3.3 states that 123123 and 321321 are shape-Wilf-equivalent, just as 1212 and 2121 are. Combined with Proposition 3.2, this means that 123=12⊕1123=12\oplus 1 is shape-Wilf-equivalent to 213=21⊕1213=21\oplus 1.

By Proposition 3.2, one way to show that two permutations α\alpha and β\beta are not shape-Wilf-equivalent is to show that α⊕1\alpha\oplus 1 and β⊕1\beta\oplus 1 are not Wilf-equivalent. Enumerating the 123⊕1123\oplus 1-, 231⊕1231\oplus 1-, and 132⊕1132\oplus 1-avoiding permutations to length 77 rules out any additional equivalences, leaving three shape-Wilf-equivalence classes of permutations of length three: {123,321,213}\{123,321,213\}, {231,312}\{231,312\}, and {132}\{132\}.

Stankova [76] showed that these equivalence classes can be ordered by avoidance: for any Ferrers board, there are at least as many 132132-avoiding frps as 321321-avoiding frps, and at least as many 321321-avoiding frps as 231231-avoiding frps. In other words, 132132 is the easiest pattern of length three to avoid on Ferrers boards of any shape, while 231231 is the hardest.

Computation shows that Proposition 3.2 together with Theorems 3.3 and 3.4 account for all shape-Wilf-equivalences of permutations of length 66 or less.

Question 3.5.

Do Proposition 3.2 and Theorems 3.3 and 3.4 imply all shape-Wilf-equivalences?

A potential converse to Proposition 3.2 was raised by Burstein at Permutation Patterns 2025.

Question 3.6 (Burstein).

If α⊕1∼β⊕1\alpha\oplus 1\sim\beta\oplus 1, must α\alpha and β\beta be shape-Wilf-equivalent?

Although most Wilf-equivalences seem to arise from shape-Wilf-equivalence, there is at least one exception. Stankova [74] proved that 1342∼24131342\sim 2413, but these permutations are not shape-Wilf-equivalent because the enumeration of 1342⊕11342\oplus 1- and 2413⊕12413\oplus 1-avoiding permutations differs at length 88. A bijective proof of this Wilf-equivalence was later given by Bloom [17].

Toward necessary conditions

While sufficient conditions for Wilf-equivalence have received considerable attention, necessary conditions have been lacking. At present, the only general method for proving that π≁σ\pi\not\sim\sigma is to enumerate the π\pi- and σ\sigma-avoiding permutations until the counts disagree. This is obviously unhelpful for proving general statements about infinite families of patterns, or for developing any structural understanding of when Wilf-equivalence fails.

A more refined approach would study permutations of small “codimension” above a pattern. For a permutation β\beta of length mm, define

gk​(β)=|{permutations of length ​m+k​ that contain ​β}|.g_{k}(\beta)\;=\;\bigl|\{\text{permutations of length }m+k\text{ that contain }\beta\}\bigr|.

Since |Avn⁡(β)|=n!−gn−m​(β)|\operatorname{Av}_{n}(\beta)|=n!-g_{n-m}(\beta), we have π∼σ\pi\sim\sigma if and only if gk​(π)=gk​(σ)g_{k}(\pi)=g_{k}(\sigma) for all kk. Thus, understanding the function gkg_{k} could yield necessary conditions for Wilf-equivalence.

For small kk, some results are known. Pratt [66, p. 276] observed in 1973 that g1​(β)=m2+1g_{1}(\beta)=m^{2}+1 for any permutation β\beta of length mm; that is, g1g_{1} depends only on the length of β\beta, not on its structure. Ray and West [68] showed that

g2​(β)=m4+2​m3+m2+4​m+4−2​j2g_{2}(\beta)\;=\;\frac{m^{4}+2m^{3}+m^{2}+4m+4-2j}{2}

for some integer jj with 0≤j≤m−10\leq j\leq m-1. However, the dependence of jj on β\beta is not well understood. The author raised the following two problems at Permutation Patterns 2007 [84].

Problem 3.7.

Express the quantity jj in the Ray–West formula for g2​(β)g_{2}(\beta) in terms of statistics of β\beta.

Problem 3.8.

Find a formula for g3​(β)g_{3}(\beta).

Unbalanced Wilf-equivalence

So far we have discussed Wilf-equivalence of individual permutations, but the notion extends naturally to sets: two sets of permutations BB and B′B^{\prime} are Wilf-equivalent if |Avn⁡(B)|=|Avn⁡(B′)||\operatorname{Av}_{n}(B)|=|\operatorname{Av}_{n}(B^{\prime})| for all nn. One might expect Wilf-equivalent sets to have the same cardinality, but this is not the case.

Atkinson, Murphy, and Ruškuc [7] characterized the class of permutations sortable by two increasing stacks in series. Its basis is infinite,

{2(2k−1) 4 1 6 3⋯(2k)(2k−3):k≥2},\{2\ (2k{-}1)\ 4\ 1\ 6\ 3\ \cdots\ (2k)\ (2k{-}3):k\geq 2\},

but they showed that the class is nonetheless Wilf-equivalent to Av⁡(1342)\operatorname{Av}(1342), which was enumerated by Bóna [20].44 4 A simpler derivation of the generating function of Av⁡(1342)\operatorname{Av}(1342) using full rook placements has since been given by Bloom and Elizalde [18, Theorem 4.3].

Burstein and Pantone [27] give further examples of such unbalanced Wilf-equivalences between finite sets, such as {1324,3416725}∼{1234}\{1324,3416725\}\sim\{1234\}. These remain poorly understood.

4. Derangements

A major focus in the study of permutation patterns has been the enumeration of specific permutation classes, especially those defined by relatively few, relatively short basis elements. Beyond mere “stamp collecting”, the ability to enumerate a class serves as a proxy for understanding its structure, and as a measuring stick for the adequacy of existing techniques. By now, however, the low-hanging fruit appears to have mostly been picked.

In particular, the “2×42\times 4” classes (those with basis consisting of two permutations of length 44) have been almost completely exhausted. These classes served for many years as a testbed for different enumerative approaches, but of the 5656 symmetry classes and 3838 Wilf-equivalence classes, only three have unknown generating functions. Moreover, Albert, Homberger, Pantone, Shar, and Vatter [2] give evidence that the generating functions for these three remaining classes do not satisfy algebraic differential equations; this would imply that they are not D-finite (not even differentially algebraic). It remains possible that these generating functions have nice continued fraction expressions, though no 2×42\times 4 class is known to have such a form.

As exact enumeration of permutation classes reaches maturity, it is natural to seek refinements that impose additional structure. One may ask, for instance, to count the alternating (up-down) permutations in a class, or the even permutations, or the Dumont permutations of the first kind, or the involutions. Many such refinements have proved tractable.

However, one type of permutation has remained stubbornly difficult to count, even in very well-behaved permutation classes: derangements. Recall that a derangement is a permutation with no fixed points (entries satisfying π⁡(i)=i\pi(i)=i, lying on the main diagonal of the plot). We survey the few known results below, but quickly reach open questions.

Derangements avoiding a pattern of length three

Robertson, Saracino, and Zeilberger [69] initiated the study of pattern-avoiding derangements. Both the inverse and reverse-complement symmetries preserve the number of fixed points, so they act as symmetries on the set of derangements. This reduces the consideration of derangements avoiding a pattern of length three to four cases: {123}\{123\}, {132,213}\{132,213\}, {231,312}\{231,312\}, and {321}\{321\}.

Robertson, Saracino, and Zeilberger proved that for β∈{132,213,321}\beta\in\{132,213,321\}, the β\beta-avoiding derangements are counted by Fine’s sequence (A000957):

0, 1, 2, 6, 18, 57, 186, 622, 2120, 7338, 25724, 91144,….0,\ 1,\ 2,\ 6,\ 18,\ 57,\ 186,\ 622,\ 2120,\ 7338,\ 25724,\ 91144,\ \dots.

The coincidence between 132132 and 321321 is surprising, since these patterns lie in different symmetry classes. Of course they are Wilf-equivalent (both avoidance classes are counted by the Catalan numbers), but the coincidence for derangements does not follow from that. In fact, Robertson, Saracino, and Zeilberger proved something stronger: the distribution of the number of fixed points is the same across all 132132-avoiding and all 321321-avoiding permutations.

Elizalde [38] strengthened this further, proving that the joint distribution of the number of fixed points and the number of excedances (entries satisfying π⁡(i)>i\pi(i)>i) is the same for 132132-avoiders and 321321-avoiders. Elizalde and Pak [40] later gave a bijective proof of this result.55 5 The chronology here is unusual: Elizalde and Pak’s bijective paper appeared in 2004, while Elizalde’s initial result, though presented at FPSAC 2003, was not formally published until 2011, in the Zeilberger Festschrift volume of the Electronic Journal of Combinatorics.

For β∈{231,312}\beta\in\{231,312\}, the β\beta-avoiding derangements are counted by A258041:

0, 1, 1, 4, 10, 31, 94, 303, 986, 3284, 11099, 38024,….0,\ 1,\ 1,\ 4,\ 10,\ 31,\ 94,\ 303,\ 986,\ 3284,\ 11099,\ 38024,\ \dots.

Robertson, Saracino, and Zeilberger compute the first eight terms of this sequence [69, Table 3], and prove [69, Theorem 7.1] that there are strictly fewer 231231-avoiding derangements than 132132-avoiding derangements of each length n≥3n\geq 3 (one might skip ahead to Figure 4; it’s not even close). Elizalde [37, Theorem 3.7] gives a continued fraction expression for the generating function for 231231-avoiding permutations according to the number of fixed points.

This leaves the case of 123123-avoiding derangements. Here the sequence begins

0, 1, 2, 7, 20, 66, 218, 725, 2538, 8646, 31118, 108430,….0,\ 1,\ 2,\ 7,\ 20,\ 66,\ 218,\ 725,\ 2538,\ 8646,\ 31118,\ 108430,\ \dots.

This is sequence A318232 in the OEIS, and that entry references the work of Fu, Tang, Han, and Zeng [41]. They define

Gn​(t)=∑πt𝖾𝗑𝖼​π,G_{n}(t)=\sum_{\pi}t^{\mathsf{exc}\,\pi},

where the sum is over 123123-avoiding derangements of length nn and 𝖾𝗑𝖼​π\mathsf{exc}\,\pi denotes the number of excedances of π\pi. In particular, Gn​(1)G_{n}(1) is the number of 123123-avoiding derangements.

Fu, Tang, Han, and Zeng also consider Gn​(−1)G_{n}(-1), for which they have a conjecture [41, Conjecture 5.11]. For odd nn, we always have Gn​(−1)=0G_{n}(-1)=0: the reverse-complement symmetry preserves 123123-avoidance and, for derangements, exchanges excedances with non-excedances. Thus if π\pi has kk excedances, its reverse-complement has n−kn-k, and when nn is odd these have opposite parities, so the contributions cancel. For even nn, they conjecture that (−1)n/2​Gn​(−1)(-1)^{n/2}G_{n}(-1) is positive. This amounts to a statement about whether, for a given even length, there are more 123123-avoiding derangements with an even number of excedances or with an odd number.

A 123123-avoiding permutation can have at most two fixed points. Elizalde [37, Corollary 3.2] shows that the enumeration of 123123-avoiding permutations by number of fixed points reduces to enumerating those with exactly two fixed points, as the other cases can be computed from this count. He gives a formula [37, Theorem 3.3] for the number of 123123-avoiding permutations with exactly two fixed points, but it involves a quadruple sum. Using this formula, Elizalde [37, Theorem 3.4] proves that for n≥4n\geq 4, there are strictly more 123123-avoiding derangements than 132132-avoiding derangements of length nn (see Figure 4). This inequality had been observed based on the data for 4≤n≤84\leq n\leq 8 by Robertson, Saracino, and Zeilberger, and Elizalde reports that it was conjectured independently by Bóna and Guibert.

A closed-form enumeration remains elusive. Elizalde [37, p. 8] notes that he has “not been able to find a satisfactory expression” for the generating function, although he expresses hope [37, p. 39] that a simpler formula than his Theorem 3.3 exists. Birmajer, Gil, Tirrell, and Weiner [16, Conjecture A.2] conjecture a simpler formula for the number of 123123-avoiding permutations with two fixed points, parameterized by the distance between the fixed points; if proved, this would reduce Elizalde’s quadruple sum to a double sum. The two formulas agree through n=200n=200.

Using the first 200200 terms, Pantone (personal communication) was able to fit a linear differential equation to the generating function, suggesting that it is D-finite. Unfortunately, that differential equation is quite unwieldy (far too long to include here). It remains possible that a nicer expression exists in the form of a continued fraction, as Elizalde [37, Theorem 3.7] found for 231231-avoiding permutations according to the number of fixed points.

Proportions

Figure 4 plots the proportion of β\beta-avoiding permutations of length nn that are derangements, for each of the three symmetry classes of patterns of length three, with nn ranging from 11 to 100100. The figure illustrates the comparisons established above: 123123-avoiding permutations are more likely to be derangements than 132132-avoiding permutations, which in turn are more likely to be derangements than 231231-avoiding permutations. It is tempting to observe that this ordering is reversed from the number of fixed points in the patterns themselves; patterns with more fixed points appear to be avoided by proportionally more derangements. Curious.

For β∈{132,213,321}{\beta\in\{132,213,321\}}, we have the Robertson, Saracino, and Zeilberger result that the β\beta-avoiding derangements are counted by Fine’s sequence. Denoting these numbers by FnF_{n}, they satisfy Cn=2​Fn+Fn−1C_{n}=2F_{n}+F_{n-1}, where CnC_{n} denotes the Catalan numbers, so Cn/Fn=2+Fn−1/FnC_{n}/F_{n}=2+F_{n-1}/F_{n}. Since the growth rate of Fine’s sequence is also 44 like the Catalan numbers, we see that Cn/Fn→9/4C_{n}/F_{n}\to\nicefrac{{9}}{{4}}, and thus Fn/Cn→4/9F_{n}/C_{n}\to\nicefrac{{4}}{{9}}.

For β=123\beta=123, Figure 4 suggests that the number of 123123-avoiding derangements grows like δ​Cn\delta C_{n} for some limiting proportion δ≥1/2\delta\geq\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}}, where CnC_{n} denotes the nnth Catalan number. Assuming this asymptotic form and using the first 200200 terms of the enumeration, Pantone (personal communication) applied the method of differential approximates to conjecture that the limiting proportion is precisely 9/16\nicefrac{{9}}{{16}}.

Conjecture 4.1 (Pantone).

The limiting proportion of derangements among 123123-avoiding permutations is equal to 9/16\nicefrac{{9}}{{16}}.

For β∈{231,312}\beta\in\{231,312\}, Figure 4 and numerical experimentation suggest that the proportion tends to 00.

Question 4.2.

Is the limiting proportion of derangements among 231231-avoiding permutations equal to 00?

These observations suggest broader questions. For a permutation class 𝒞\mathcal{C}, let 𝒞∘\mathcal{C}^{\circ} denote the set of derangements in 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

Question 4.3.

Does the ratio |𝒞n∘|/|𝒞n||\mathcal{C}^{\circ}_{n}|/|\mathcal{C}_{n}| converge for every permutation class 𝒞\mathcal{C}?

Numerous follow-up questions suggest themselves. For the class of all permutations, the limit is of course 1/e\nicefrac{{1}}{{e}}. What values in [0,1][0,1] are achievable? The case of Av⁡(132)\operatorname{Av}(132) shows that these limits can be greater than 1/e\nicefrac{{1}}{{e}}, but how much greater? Is there a largest possible limit strictly less than 11? For which classes is this limit 00?

Separable derangements

The skew sum of permutations σ\sigma of length mm and τ\tau of length nn is the permutation σ⊖τ\sigma\ominus\tau of length m+n{m+n} defined by

(σ⊖τ)​(i)={σ⁡(i)+nfor ​1≤i≤m,τ⁡(i−m)for ​m+1≤i≤m+n.(\sigma\ominus\tau)(i)\;=\;\begin{cases}\sigma(i)+n&\text{for }1\leq i\leq m,\\ \tau(i-m)&\text{for }m+1\leq i\leq m+n.\end{cases}

Visually, the plot of σ⊖τ\sigma\ominus\tau places the plot of τ\tau below and to the right of the plot of σ\sigma.

A permutation is separable if it can be built from the singleton permutation 11 by repeated application of sum and skew sum. Bose, Buss, and Lubiw [25] gave the separable permutations their name and showed that they are precisely Av⁡(2413,3142)\operatorname{Av}(2413,3142). Notable subclasses include Av⁡(132)\operatorname{Av}(132) and Av⁡(231)\operatorname{Av}(231), which we have just discussed, as well as the layered permutations discussed earlier. The separable permutations of length nn are counted by the large Schröder numbers (A006318):

1, 2, 6, 22, 90, 394, 1806, 8558, 41586, 206098, 1037718, 5293446,….1,\ 2,\ 6,\ 22,\ 90,\ 394,\ 1806,\ 8558,\ 41586,\ 206098,\ 1037718,\ 5293446,\ \dots.

This enumeration was first established by Shapiro and Stephens [72] in 1991, though they worked with the recursive definition via sums and skew sums. This was before Bose, Buss, and Lubiw had identified the basis {2413,3142}\{2413,3142\}, which led to an amusing historical coincidence: As West [88] reports, Shapiro and Getu later conjectured that the large Schröder numbers also count Av⁡(2413,3142)\operatorname{Av}(2413,3142), not realizing Shapiro had already proved this himself, albeit in a disguised form. West [88] gave a proof in 1995.66 6 West wrote that this was “the first non-trivial enumerative result to be obtained for any problem involving forbidden subsequences of length k≥4k\geq 4.” This overlooks Gessel’s 1990 paper [44], which gives an explicit formula for 12341234-avoiding permutations. Since [44] is cited in [88], this is a puzzling omission; perhaps West meant the first involving non-monotone patterns, or more than one pattern. Stankova [74] then gave the much more natural proof, decomposing these permutations into sums and skew sums, which brings the story full circle to Shapiro and Stephens.

For classes with only finitely many simple permutations (a term we won’t define here), such as the separable permutations, Brignall, Huczynska, and Vatter [26] show how to systematically obtain algebraic equations for the generating functions of various natural subsets: the alternating permutations, the even permutations, the Dumont permutations of the first kind, the involutions, and many others. However, their method does not apply to derangements. The obstacle is that being a derangement does not lie in a finite “query-complete set of properties” (in the sense of that paper). The proof of this fact uses displacement sets, D⁡(π)={π⁡(i)−i:i∈[n]}D(\pi)=\{\pi(i)-i:i\in[n]\}, so a permutation π\pi is a derangement if and only if 0∉D⁡(π)0\notin D(\pi). While D⁡(π⊕σ)=D⁡(π)∪D⁡(σ)D(\pi\oplus\sigma)=D(\pi)\cup D(\sigma), whether a skew sum π⊖σ\pi\ominus\sigma is a derangement depends on the interaction between D⁡(π)D(\pi) and D⁡(σ)D(\sigma), and so permutations with different displacement sets must be tracked separately.

Thus despite the well-understood structure of separable permutations, no explicit expression for the generating function of separable derangements has been found. These permutations are counted by A393394,

0, 1, 2, 7, 30, 124, 560, 2610, 12470, 60955, 302930, 1528621,….0,\ 1,\ 2,\ 7,\ 30,\ 124,\ 560,\ 2610,\ 12470,\ 60955,\ 302930,\ 1528621,\ \dots.

These terms were computed by tracking, for each length, how many separable permutations realize each possible displacement set. The count of separable derangements is then the sum over displacement sets not containing 00.

Problem 4.4.

Find the generating function for the number of separable derangements of length nn.

The ratios |𝒮n∘|/|𝒮n||\mathcal{S}^{\circ}_{n}|/|\mathcal{S}_{n}|, where 𝒮\mathcal{S} denotes the class of separable permutations, appear to be monotonically decreasing, approaching something between 1/5\nicefrac{{1}}{{5}} and 1/4\nicefrac{{1}}{{4}}. However, these guesses are based only on the enumeration up to length 1818 and so should be taken with a grain of salt.

Question 4.5.

What is the limiting proportion of derangements among separable permutations, assuming this limit exists?

5. Sorting

The study of sorting devices has been intertwined with permutation patterns since Knuth’s analysis of stack-sorting in The Art of Computer Programming. In this section, we consider several sorting machines: multiple stacks in series, Atkinson’s enhanced (r,s)(r,s)-stacks, and restricted containers (also known as 𝒞\mathcal{C}-machines). Each machine gives rise to a permutation class (the permutations it can sort/generate), and there are numerous open problems.

Stacks

A stack is a last-in first-out linear sorting device with push and pop operations. The greedy algorithm for stack-sorting a permutation π=π(1)π(2)⋯π(n)\pi=\pi(1)\pi(2)\cdots\pi(n) proceeds as follows. First, push π⁡(1)\pi(1) onto the stack. At a later stage, suppose that the entries π⁡(1),…,π⁡(i−1)\pi(1),\dots,\pi(i-1) have all been either output or pushed onto the stack, so π⁡(i)\pi(i) is the next entry in the input. If π⁡(i)\pi(i) is less than every entry currently on the stack, push π⁡(i)\pi(i) onto the stack. Otherwise, pop entries off the stack (to the output) until π⁡(i)\pi(i) is less than every remaining stack entry, then push π⁡(i)\pi(i) onto the stack. After all entries have been read, pop any remaining entries from the stack to the output. This produces a permutation s⁡(π)s(\pi).

A permutation is West tt-stack sortable if st​(π)s^{t}(\pi) is the identity permutation. We caution that for t≥2{t\geq 2}, the set of West-tt-stack-sortable permutations does not form a permutation class. As one example, 3524135241 is West-22-stack-sortable, because

s⁡(s⁡(35241))=s⁡(32145)=12345,s(s(35241))=s(32145)=12345,

but its subpermutation 32413241 is not West-22-stack-sortable, because

s⁡(s⁡(3241))=s⁡(2314)=2134≠1234.s(s(3241))=s(2314)=2134\neq 1234.

Indeed, West [86, Theorem 4.2.18] (and later in [87]) showed that the West-22-stack-sortable permutations (he did not call them this) are characterized by avoiding 23412341 in the standard sense, and also avoiding the barred pattern 3​5¯​2413\overline{5}241; a permutation avoids 3​5¯​2413\overline{5}241 if every occurrence of the pattern 32413241 can be extended to an occurrence of the pattern 3524135241.

We will not belabor West stack-sorting any further, and instead turn to sorting with tt stacks in series: a permutation is sortable by tt stacks in series if there exists some sequence of operations that transforms it into the identity, where each operation pushes to or pops from one of the tt stacks, and entries pass through the stacks in order (from the first stack to the second, and so on). Unlike the West notion, this definition behaves as one might reasonably hope. In particular, the set of permutations sortable by tt stacks in series forms a permutation class: if a permutation can be sorted, then any subpermutation can be sorted by running the same operations while ignoring the entries not present in the subpermutation.

One and two stacks

The permutations sortable by a single stack are precisely Av⁡(231)\operatorname{Av}(231), as observed by Knuth [51, Exercise 2.2.1-5]. For two stacks in series, Tarjan [82, Lemma 10] found that the shortest unsortable permutation has length 77. We quote his ‘‘proof’’77 7 Pratt [66], in a paper from the same era, begins a proof with “We leave to the reader the pleasure of convincing himself that none of the permutations in Figure 3 can be computed by a deque.” The implicit assumption in both papers, one published in the Journal of the ACM and the other in STOC, that the reader would verify such claims by hand rather than by computer is now somewhat quaint.:

(2435761)(2435761) is unsortable using two stacks, as the reader may easily verify. Conversely, every sequence of length 66 or less may be sorted using two stacks. Exhaustive case analysis will verify this fact.

In a 1992 technical report [4, Theorem 2], Atkinson seems to have been the first to find all 2222 basis elements of length 77 for two stacks in series. Murphy [62, Proposition 257] proved that the class of permutations sortable by two stacks in series has an infinite basis, and in addition to the 2222 basis elements of length 77, he lists the 5151 basis elements of length 88. More generally, the number of basis elements of length nn, for n≥7n\geq 7, is given by A111576:

22, 51, 146, 604,….22,\ 51,\ 146,\ 604,\ \dots.

Computing these basis elements up to n=10n=10 is not difficult once one views the sortable permutations in terms of products of 231231-avoiding permutations, as we explain below.

Sorting, generating, and duality

We pause to discuss a general framework that clarifies several arguments to follow. We think of sorting machines as transforming an input permutation (generally drawn on the right in diagrams, so that the entries enter the machine in their natural order π⁡(1)\pi(1), π⁡(2)\pi(2), …\dots) to an output permutation. Sorting is then the special case where the output is the identity.

Generating is the special case where the input is the identity.

A machine is symbol oblivious if its allowed operations are indifferent to the values of the symbols being manipulated. (This terminology follows Atkinson [6], although he simply uses oblivious; we add ‘‘symbol’’ to avoid confusion with other uses of the term ‘‘oblivious’’ in computer science.) A stack is symbol oblivious: a push or pop is permitted regardless of what symbol is involved.88 8 Although not under West’s notion, since the rule “pop if the top of the stack is smaller than the next input entry” depends on comparing symbol values. Compositions of stacks in series are also symbol oblivious.

For a symbol-oblivious machine, if we relabel the input symbols and perform the same sequence of operations, we obtain the correspondingly relabeled output. Suppose a symbol-oblivious machine MM can transform π\pi into σ\sigma. Relabeling by an arbitrary permutation τ\tau shows that the same sequence of operations allows MM to transform τ∘π\tau\circ\pi into τ∘σ\tau\circ\sigma. In particular, taking τ=σ−1\tau=\sigma^{-1}, we see that MM can transform σ−1∘π\sigma^{-1}\circ\pi into the identity. In other words:

Proposition 5.1.

Let MM be a symbol-oblivious machine. Then MM can transform π\pi into σ\sigma if and only if MM can sort σ−1∘π\sigma^{-1}\circ\pi. In particular, MM can generate π\pi if and only if MM can sort π−1\pi^{-1}.

For example, a single stack sorts precisely the class Av⁡(231)\operatorname{Av}(231). Since 312−1=231312^{-1}=231, Proposition 5.1 implies that a single stack generates the class Av⁡(312)\operatorname{Av}(312) from the identity.

More generally, symbol obliviousness clarifies what two stacks in series can generate. Suppose entries pass through the first stack and enter the second stack in the order σ⁡(1),σ⁡(2),…,σ⁡(n)\sigma(1),\sigma(2),\ldots,\sigma(n). Since a single stack generates Av⁡(312)\operatorname{Av}(312), we have σ∈Av⁡(312)\sigma\in\operatorname{Av}(312). By symbol obliviousness, the second stack performs some sequence of operations that would transform 12⋯n12\cdots n into some τ∈Av⁡(312)\tau\in\operatorname{Av}(312). Since the actual symbols input into the second stack are σ⁡(1),…,σ⁡(n)\sigma(1),\ldots,\sigma(n) rather than 1,…,n1,\ldots,n, the output is relabeled accordingly, generating σ∘τ\sigma\circ\tau. Thus two stacks in series generate precisely Av⁡(312)∘Av⁡(312)\operatorname{Av}(312)\circ\operatorname{Av}(312).

This yields a simple method for computing the basis mentioned earlier: generate all elements of Av⁡(231)∘Av⁡(231)\operatorname{Av}(231)\circ\operatorname{Av}(231) up to the desired length, and identify the minimal permutations that do not appear.

A second useful observation concerns running machines backwards. Suppose that a machine MM can transform π\pi into σ\sigma via some sequence of operations.

Reading that sequence backwards describes a way for a “reversed machine” MrM^{\mathrm{r}} to transform σr\sigma^{\mathrm{r}} into πr\pi^{\mathrm{r}}.

In general, MrM^{\mathrm{r}} may be a different machine than MM, and we say that MM is reversible if Mr=MM^{\mathrm{r}}=M. Stacks in series are reversible (reverse the roles of input and output, reverse the order of the stacks, and exchange pushes with pops).

If we assume that MM, and hence also MrM^{\mathrm{r}}, is symbol oblivious, and that MM can sort π\pi, then MrM^{\mathrm{r}} can transform ρ=n(n−1)⋯21\rho=n(n-1)\cdots 21 into πr\pi^{\mathrm{r}}.

Relabeling the entries according to (πr)−1(\pi^{\mathrm{r}})^{-1}, we see that MrM^{\mathrm{r}} transforms (πr)−1∘ρ=ρ∘π−1∘ρ=(πrc)−1(\pi^{\mathrm{r}})^{-1}\circ\rho=\rho\circ\pi^{-1}\circ\rho=(\pi^{\mathrm{rc}})^{-1} into the identity, which we record below.

Proposition 5.2.

If a symbol-oblivious machine MM can sort π\pi, then the reversed machine MrM^{\mathrm{r}} can sort (πrc)−1=ρ∘π−1∘ρ(\pi^{\mathrm{rc}})^{-1}=\rho\circ\pi^{-1}\circ\rho.

Since stacks in series are symbol oblivious and reversible, if π\pi can be sorted by tt stacks in series, then (πrc)−1(\pi^{\mathrm{rc}})^{-1} can also be sorted by tt stacks in series. As Figure 2 shows, the permutation (πrc)−1(\pi^{\mathrm{rc}})^{-1} is the reflection of π\pi about the anti-diagonal. This permutation has been called the “dual” of π\pi (Murphy [62, Section 8.1.2]) or the “two-stack dual” (Smith and Vatter [73]). We suggest instead the term sorting dual, since this duality applies to any symbol-oblivious reversible machine.

General bounds

For general tt, Knuth presents an argument in The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 3 [52, Solution to Exercise 5.2.4-19] showing that if all permutations of length nn can be sorted by tt stacks in series, then all permutations of length 2​n2n can be sorted by t+1t+1 stacks in series. (This argument also appears in Tarjan [82, Lemma 11].)

We sketch the proof. Let π\pi be a permutation of length 2​n2n and suppose that all permutations of length nn can be sorted by tt stacks in series. By symbol-obliviousness, all permutations of length nn can be transformed into ρ=n(n−1)⋯21\rho=n(n-1)\cdots 21. Thus we can use the first tt of our t+1t+1 stacks to output π⁡(1),…,π⁡(n)\pi(1),\dots,\pi(n) in descending order, pushing these entries into the last stack so that they sit in increasing order (read top to bottom) before we read π⁡(n+1)\pi(n+1). We then use the first tt stacks to sort π⁡(n+1),…,π⁡(2​n)\pi(n+1),\dots,\pi(2n), merging these entries with the contents of the final stack into the output as desired.

Murphy [62, Proposition 264] gives a different argument to obtain a similar result. In his approach, we process all entries π⁡(1),…,π⁡(2​n)\pi(1),\dots,\pi(2n) at once. The entries with values 1,2,…,n1,2,\dots,n are sorted and output using the last tt stacks (these are pushed onto the first stack but immediately popped off it). The entries with values n+1,n+2,…,2​nn+1,n+2,\dots,2n are pushed into the first stack, where they remain temporarily. Once all entries with values 1,2,…,n1,2,\dots,n have been output, the entries n+1,n+2,…,2​nn+1,n+2,\dots,2n sit “upside down” in the first stack, in the reverse order of the subsequence they form in π\pi, read top to bottom. We then sort and output these using the last tt stacks.

In fact, Knuth’s argument and Murphy’s argument are the sorting duals of each other. Suppose that the permutations π\pi and σ\sigma can be sorted by tt stacks in series. Knuth’s argument shows that t+1{t+1} stacks in series can sort all horizontal juxtapositions of the form [ρ∘πσ]\begin{bmatrix}\rho\circ\pi&\sigma\end{bmatrix}: permutations of length |π|+|σ|{|\pi|+|\sigma|} in which the first |π||\pi| entries are order-isomorphic to ρ∘π\rho\circ\pi (the complement of π\pi) and the last |σ||\sigma| entries are order-isomorphic to σ\sigma. Murphy’s argument shows that t+1t+1 stacks in series can sort all vertical juxtapositions of the form [π∘ρσ]T\begin{bmatrix}\pi\circ\rho&\sigma\end{bmatrix}^{\mathrm{T}}: permutations of length |π|+|σ||\pi|+|\sigma| in which the largest |π||\pi| values are order-isomorphic to π∘ρ\pi\circ\rho (the reverse of π\pi) and the smallest |σ||\sigma| values are order-isomorphic to σ\sigma.

To see the duality, substitute the sorting duals of π\pi and σ\sigma into Murphy’s construction. Since the sorting dual of π\pi is ρ∘π−1∘ρ\rho\circ\pi^{-1}\circ\rho, we obtain vertical juxtapositions of the form

[(ρ∘π−1∘ρ)∘ρρ∘σ−1∘ρ]=[ρ∘π−1ρ∘σ−1∘ρ].\begin{bmatrix}(\rho\circ\pi^{-1}\circ\rho)\circ\rho\\[4.0pt] \rho\circ\sigma^{-1}\circ\rho\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\rho\circ\pi^{-1}\\[4.0pt] \rho\circ\sigma^{-1}\circ\rho\end{bmatrix}.

The sorting duals of these permutations are precisely the horizontal juxtapositions from Knuth’s argument.

Since two stacks in series can sort every permutation of length 66, it follows from these constructions that t≥2t\geq 2 stacks in series can sort every permutation of length 3⋅2t−13\cdot 2^{t-1}. Atkinson [4, Corollary, p.10] refined this bound to 7⋅2t−2−17\cdot 2^{t-2}-1, but the asymptotics are the same: roughly log2⁡n\log_{2}n stacks in series suffice to sort all permutations of length nn.

For a lower bound, observe that a single stack can sort precisely CnC_{n} permutations of length nn, where CnC_{n} denotes the nnth Catalan number. Thus tt stacks in series can sort at most CntC_{n}^{t} permutations of length nn. This shows that roughly log4⁡n\log_{4}n stacks in series are required to sort all permutations of length nn.

There is a factor-of-two gap between these bounds, and it has not been significantly narrowed since Knuth first posed the following problem almost sixty years ago, which he rated 4747 out of 5050 in difficulty.

Problem 5.3 (Knuth [52, Exercise 5.2.4-20]).

Determine the true rate of growth, as n→∞n\to\infty, of the number of stacks in series needed to sort every permutation of length nn.

Three stacks

Specializing to three stacks, we immediately run into problems. The exhaustive computational approach that works for two stacks becomes intractable, as computing

Av⁡(231)∘Av⁡(231)∘Av⁡(231)\operatorname{Av}(231)\circ\operatorname{Av}(231)\circ\operatorname{Av}(231)

for even modest lengths is infeasible. We do not even know the length of the shortest basis element for the class of 33-stack-sortable permutations, although Atkinson’s bound shows that all permutations of length 7⋅2−1=137\cdot 2-1=13 can be sorted, so this shortest basis element must have length at least 1414. Elder and Vatter [36] report that Elder and Waton wagered a beer on the problem, with Elder guessing 1515 and Waton guessing 2222 (“conjecturing,” if one is feeling generous).

Question 5.4 (Waton; see Elder and Vatter [36]).

What is the length of the shortest permutation that cannot be sorted by three stacks in series?

Murphy [62, Conjecture 265] guesses more generally that tt stacks in series can sort all permutations of length up to (t+1)!(t+1)!, which would give 2525 as the length of the shortest permutation unsortable by three stacks in series. However, Murphy’s conjecture can’t be true for all tt, since log4⁡(t+1)!\log_{4}(t+1)! grows faster than tt.

The known unsortable permutations are shockingly long, given these conjectured answers. Tarjan [82] reports that he constructed a permutation of length 4141 that cannot be sorted by three stacks in series, although he doesn’t present it. Murphy [62, Proposition 262] gives a general method to construct permutations that cannot be sorted by t+1t+1 stacks in series, starting from a permutation that cannot be sorted by tt stacks. We sketch his argument.

Suppose that some permutation β\beta of length kk cannot be sorted by tt stacks in series. Consider the permutation

π=β⁡[βr,βr,…,βr⏟|β|−1 copies,1],\pi\;=\;\beta[\,\underbrace{\,\beta^{\mathrm{r}},\,\beta^{\mathrm{r}},\dots,\,\beta^{\mathrm{r}}}_{\text{$|\beta|-1$ copies}},1\,],

the inflation of β\beta formed, loosely speaking, by replacing each entry of β\beta except the last with a block of entries order-isomorphic to βr\beta^{\mathrm{r}}. We claim that π\pi cannot be sorted by t+1t+1 stacks in series. Indeed, we can never have all entries from a single βr\beta^{\mathrm{r}} interval together in the first stack, because reading top to bottom they would form a copy of β\beta, and the remaining tt stacks could not sort them. Thus at least one entry from the first interval must exit the first stack before the first entry of the second interval enters, and similarly for subsequent intervals. Focusing on these |β|−1|\beta|-1 entries together with the final entry of π\pi, we obtain a subsequence order-isomorphic to β\beta that enters the last tt stacks in that order, and the last tt stacks cannot sort β\beta, so they cannot sort this subsequence.

Murphy’s construction yields an unsortable permutation of length |β|2−|β|+1|\beta|^{2}-|\beta|+1. For three stacks, we start with a permutation of length 77 (the shortest length not sortable by two stacks), giving an unsortable permutation of length 4343, which is longer than Tarjan’s claimed example. Murphy [62, p. 329] examines one such permutation and finds four entries that can be removed without making it sortable, yielding an unsortable permutation of length 3939. In his 1992 technical report, Atkinson [4, Lemma 5] had already done much the same, although he obtained an unsortable permutation of length 3838. This record has stood for over thirty years.

Atkinson’s (r,s)(r,s)-stacks

In a 1998 paper, Atkinson [5] introduced a natural generalization of stacks. With a standard stack, one may push an entry onto the top or pop an entry from the top. An (r,s)(r,s)-stack relaxes these constraints: one may push the next input entry into any of the top rr positions and pop any of the top ss entries to the output. Thus a (1,1)(1,1)-stack is an ordinary stack.

These machines are symbol oblivious, as their operations do not depend on the values of the entries, and the reverse of an (r,s)(r,s)-stack is an (s,r)(s,r)-stack. Thus, by Proposition 5.2, we obtain the following.

Proposition 5.5 (Atkinson [5, Lemma 1.1]).

An (r,s)(r,s)-stack sorts π\pi if and only if an (s,r)(s,r)-stack sorts its sorting dual (πrc)−1(\pi^{\mathrm{rc}})^{-1}.

In particular, the class of permutations sortable by an (r,r)(r,r)-stack is closed under the sorting dual. We return to (r,s)(r,s)-stacks later in this section.

Restricted containers (𝒞\mathcal{C}-machines)

We now introduce a different generalization of stacks that captures many permutation classes. As we will see, this framework includes Atkinson’s (r,1)(r,1)- and (1,s)(1,s)-stacks as special cases.

Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be a permutation class. A 𝒞\mathcal{C}-machine is a container that holds entries subject to the constraint that, at all times, the entries in the container (read left to right) must be order-isomorphic to a member of 𝒞\mathcal{C}. In analyzing these machines, it turns out to be more natural to study generation than sorting; we discuss this choice further below. Thus we take the input to be 12⋯n12\cdots n, and the machine has three operations:

  • •

    push: remove the next entry from the input and place it anywhere in the container, provided the resulting arrangement is order-isomorphic to a member of 𝒞\mathcal{C};

  • •

    pop: remove the leftmost entry from the container and append it to the output;

  • •

    bypass: remove the next entry from the input and append it directly to the output.

The permutation generated by a sequence of operations is the output once all entries have exited.

The classical stack is recovered by taking 𝒞=Av⁡(12)\mathcal{C}=\operatorname{Av}(12). In this machine, entries in the container must be decreasing, so each push places the new entry on the left. Since pops also occur from the left, the bypass operation is redundant, and we recover the usual stack operations. As Knuth observed, this machine generates precisely Av⁡(312)\operatorname{Av}(312).

By contrast, for the Av⁡(21)\operatorname{Av}(21)-machine, the entries in the container must be increasing, so each push places the new entry on the right. Since pops occur from the left, the bypass operation is now essential. This machine generates precisely Av⁡(321)\operatorname{Av}(321): clearly it cannot generate 321321 or any permutation containing it, and conversely, to generate a 321321-avoiding permutation, output the left-to-right maxima with bypasses while passing the remaining entries (which must be increasing) through the container. (This is equivalent to generating with two queues in parallel.)

At the other extreme, taking 𝒞\mathcal{C} to be the class of all permutations allows entries to be placed anywhere in the container, and this machine generates all permutations.

The bypass operation is superfluous in some cases, as the stack example shows. However, including it greatly simplifies the basis theorem below. In practice, bypasses are used precisely to output the left-to-right maxima of the generated permutation.

The basis theorem

The main structural result for 𝒞\mathcal{C}-machines characterizes the classes they generate and makes it immediately apparent whether a class of interest can be generated by a 𝒞\mathcal{C}-machine, and if so, which one. The proof is too simple to omit. In the statement, we use the notation 1⊖B={1⊖β:β∈B}1\ominus B=\{1\ominus\beta:\beta\in B\}.

Theorem 5.6 (Albert, Homberger, Pantone, Shar, and Vatter [2, Theorem 1.1]).

For any set BB of permutations, the Av⁡(B)\operatorname{Av}(B)-machine generates the class Av⁡(1⊖B)\operatorname{Av}(1\ominus B).

Proof.

The Av⁡(B)\operatorname{Av}(B)-machine cannot generate any permutation of the form 1⊖β1\ominus\beta for β∈B\beta\in B: at the moment when the maximum entry (which appears first in 1⊖β1\ominus\beta) is next in the input, the container would need to hold a copy of β\beta, and it is not allowed to do so.

For the converse, we show how to generate a permutation π\pi that avoids all permutations in 1⊖B1\ominus B. Let i1<i2<⋯<iℓi_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{\ell} be the positions of the left-to-right maxima of π\pi; note that i1=1i_{1}=1 since the first entry is always a left-to-right maximum.

We proceed iteratively through the left-to-right maxima. For the first, we push all entries with values less than π⁡(i1)\pi(i_{1}) into the container in their correct relative order with respect to π\pi. This is possible because the entries lying to the southeast of π⁡(i1)\pi(i_{1}) in π\pi avoid BB. We then bypass π⁡(i1)\pi(i_{1}) to the output.

For each subsequent left-to-right maximum, observe that all entries lying horizontally between the previous left-to-right maximum and the current one are already in the container. We pop these entries to the output. Then we push the entries with values between the two maxima from the input into the container, placing them in their correct relative positions with respect to π\pi. Again, this is possible because the entries lying to the southeast of the current left-to-right maximum must avoid BB. We then bypass the current maximum to the output, and repeat. ∎

Sorting versus generating

Unlike stacks, 𝒞\mathcal{C}-machines are not even a little bit symbol oblivious: the available push operations depend entirely on the relative order of the entries in the container and the next entry to be input. Thus, we can’t lean on Proposition 5.1 to conclude that sorting and generating are symmetric. What would happen if we tried to sort with a 𝒞\mathcal{C}-machine?

One answer is that sorting with 𝒞\mathcal{C}-machines, as defined, would not be all that interesting. The only productive container configuration is increasing order, since any inversion in the container would persist to the output, resulting in a failure to sort. It follows that sorting with a 𝒞\mathcal{C}-machine is equivalent to sorting with a priority queue, in which one may push and pop entries, but instead of the last-in being popped (as in a stack) or the first-in being popped (as in a queue), the least-in, that is, the smallest entry, is popped. A priority queue of unlimited capacity can sort any permutation: simply push all the entries in, then pop them out in order.99 9 The more interesting questions about priority queues concern the pairs (π,σ)(\pi,\sigma) for which a priority queue can transform π\pi into σ\sigma. A theorem of Atkinson and Thiyagarajah [8] states that there are precisely (n+1)n−1(n+1)^{n-1} such pairs of permutations of length nn. Thus if 𝒞\mathcal{C} contains the identity of all lengths, the 𝒞\mathcal{C}-machine can sort everything.

If 𝒞\mathcal{C} contains identity permutations only up to some length kk, then sorting with the 𝒞\mathcal{C}-machine is equivalent to sorting with a (k+1)(k+1)-bounded priority queue, which can hold at most k+1k+1 entries at any time. (The “+1+1” accounts for the bypass operation.) Bounded priority queues have been studied by Atkinson and Tulley [9], among others, though their sorting capabilities do not seem to have been written down explicitly. It is not difficult to see that a (k+1)(k+1)-bounded priority queue can sort precisely the class Av⁡(Sk+1⊖1)\operatorname{Av}(S_{k+1}\ominus 1), that is, the permutations avoiding all patterns of length k+2{k+2} that end with 11. Another way to describe this class is that it consists of the permutations with maximum drop size at most kk, where the maximum drop size of π\pi is max⁡{i−π⁡(i)}\max\{i-\pi(i)\}. These classes are already very well understood; in fact, Chung, Claesson, Dukes, and Graham [30] have even determined their descent polynomials. In short, sorting with 𝒞\mathcal{C}-machines as defined does not lead anywhere new.

An alternative approach to sorting with 𝒞\mathcal{C}-machines would be to modify the definition of the machines to make sorting more natural. If a 𝒞\mathcal{C}-machine can generate π\pi, then the reversed 𝒞\mathcal{C}-machine (which pushes only at the left but allows pops from anywhere in the container) can transform πr\pi^{\mathrm{r}} into idr\mathrm{id}^{\mathrm{r}}. By applying appropriate symmetries to 𝒞\mathcal{C}, one could therefore study sorting by reversed 𝒞\mathcal{C}-machines instead of generating by 𝒞\mathcal{C}-machines. But this is clearly symmetric to generating with 𝒞\mathcal{C}-machines, and generating is easier to talk about.

Atkinson’s (r,1)(r,1)- and (1,s)(1,s)-stacks as 𝒞\mathcal{C}-machines

An (r,1)(r,1)-stack allows pushing into any of the top rr positions but only popping from the top. By “rotating” this stack 90∘90^{\circ} counterclockwise, we see that it is equivalent to the Av⁡(B)\operatorname{Av}(B)-machine where BB consists of all permutations of length r+1r+1 that end with their largest entry. This allows one to insert the next entry from the input (which is larger than every entry currently in the container) into any of the first rr positions of the container, and then to pop from the first position of the container. Letting SrS_{r} denote the set of all permutations of length rr, we see that the (r,1)(r,1)-stack is equivalent to the Av⁡(Sr⊕1)\operatorname{Av}(S_{r}\oplus 1)-machine. By Theorem 5.6, this machine generates the class Av⁡(1⊖(Sr⊕1))\operatorname{Av}\bigl(1\ominus(S_{r}\oplus 1)\bigr), which reproves a result of Atkinson [5, Theorem 2.1]. By the duality of Proposition 5.5, (1,s)(1,s)-stacks are also equivalent to 𝒞\mathcal{C}-machines.

Atkinson [5, Section 3] went on to enumerate these classes, finding their algebraic generating functions and asymptotics. The enumeration of these classes also appears implicitly in the work of Kremer [54, 55], who considers, for each r≥1r\geq 1 and fixed indices j,k∈[r+2]j,k\in[r+2], classes with bases

Bj,k={β∈Sr+2:β⁡(j)=r+1 and β⁡(k)=r+2}.B_{j,k}=\{\beta\in S_{r+2}:\text{$\beta(j)=r+1$ and $\beta(k)=r+2$}\}.

Her main result [55, Theorem 1] shows that all classes of the form Av⁡(Bj,k)\operatorname{Av}(B_{j,k}) with |j−k|≤2|j-k|\leq 2, or k=1k=1, or k=r+2k=r+2, have isomorphic generating trees, and thus are Wilf-equivalent. The underlying recurrences also appear in Sulanke’s work [81] on coloured parallelogram polyominoes. (We caution readers that Kremer’s generating function as printed contains errors; Atkinson’s paper should be consulted for the correct generating function.) For r=1r=1, we obtain the Catalan numbers. For r=2r=2, the enumeration gives the large Schröder numbers (A006318), which arose earlier in this paper in the context of separable permutations; Kremer’s classes are Wilf-equivalent to the separable permutations but not symmetric to them. For r=3r=3, we obtain A054872.

Sorting 13421342-avoiders

As mentioned in Section 3, Atkinson, Murphy, and Ruškuc [7] showed that the class sortable by two ordered stacks in series is Wilf-equivalent to Av⁡(1342)\operatorname{Av}(1342). Here an ordered stack is one where the contents must remain increasing when read from top to bottom; in sorting with stacks in series, the final stack must always be ordered, but the previous stacks do not need to be. At Permutation Patterns 2007, Bóna asked [84, Question 4]:

Is there a natural sorting machine that can sort precisely the class Av⁡(1342)\operatorname{Av}(1342)?

Theorem 5.6 shows that the answer is essentially yes: the class Av⁡(4213)\operatorname{Av}(4213) is generated by the Av⁡(213)\operatorname{Av}(213)-machine. Here we have replaced Av⁡(1342)\operatorname{Av}(1342) by a symmetry and also swapped sorting for generating, but neither change is substantive. However, what Bóna actually had in mind was a more satisfying machine-level explanation of the Wilf-equivalence, and that remains open:

Problem 5.7.

Find a bijection between Av⁡(1342)\operatorname{Av}(1342) and the class sortable by two ordered stacks in series that is witnessed by a correspondence between the operation sequences of the associated machines.

Enumeration and D-finiteness

The 𝒞\mathcal{C}-machine framework leads to functional equations for generating functions. In favorable cases, these yield explicit formulas; in others, they allow efficient computation of many terms via dynamic programming.

A striking example is Av⁡(4231,4123,4312)\operatorname{Av}(4231,4123,4312).
