This class can be generated by a 𝒞\mathcal{C}-machine (all basis elements begin with their maximum entries), and Albert, Homberger, Pantone, Shar, and Vatter [2] computed 50005000 terms of its counting sequence. Despite this abundance of data, no algebraic differential equation satisfied by the generating function has been found.

The counterexamples to the Noonan–Zeilberger conjecture [63] constructed by Garrabrant and Pak [43] have extremely large bases. A more compact counterexample would be nice to have, and Av⁡(4231,4123,4312)\operatorname{Av}(4231,4123,4312), with its basis of just three short permutations, appears to be a strong candidate.

Conjecture 5.8 (Albert, Homberger, Pantone, Shar, and Vatter [2, Conjecture 5.3]).

The generating function for Av⁡(4231,4123,4312)\operatorname{Av}(4231,4123,4312) is not differentially algebraic.

Amusingly, the superclass Av⁡(4231,4312)\operatorname{Av}(4231,4312) is enumerated by the large Schröder numbers. This was conjectured by Stanley and first proved by Kremer [54, Proposition 11], although this class is not a member of her large family of Wilf-equivalent classes. Instead, she showed specifically that the generating tree for the symmetric class Av⁡(2134,1324)\operatorname{Av}(2134,1324) is isomorphic to the generating trees of her large family.

The class Av⁡(4231)\operatorname{Av}(4231), meanwhile, is symmetric to the notorious class Av⁡(1324)\operatorname{Av}(1324) mentioned in the introduction. The current record for enumerating this class is 5050 terms, computed by Conway, Guttmann, and Zinn-Justin [34]. Thus in the chain

Av⁡(4231,4123,4312)⊆Av⁡(4231,4312)⊆Av⁡(4231),\operatorname{Av}(4231,4123,4312)\;\subseteq\;\operatorname{Av}(4231,4312)\;\subseteq\;\operatorname{Av}(4231),

the first class is computationally tractable but its generating function appears poorly behaved, the second has an algebraic generating function, and no one knows what to do with the third.

The (2,2)(2,2)-stack

Returning to Atkinson’s (r,s)(r,s)-stacks, the (2,2)(2,2)-stack is the simplest case not captured by the 𝒞\mathcal{C}-machine framework: it allows pushing into either of the top two positions and popping from either of the top two positions. Atkinson established the basis for this class.

Theorem 5.9 (Atkinson [5, Theorem 4.1]).

The class of (2,2)(2,2)-stack-sortable permutations is

Av⁡(23451, 23541, 32451, 32541, 245163, 246153, 425163, 426153).\operatorname{Av}(23451,\,23541,\,32451,\,32541,\,245163,\,246153,\,425163,\,426153).

By Proposition 5.5, this class is closed under the sorting dual. This can also be seen from the basis, as every element appears alongside its sorting dual:

permutation 23451 23541 32541 245163 246153 426153
sorting dual itself 32451 itself itself 425163 itself

It would of course be desirable to have a general description of the basis of (r,s)(r,s)-stack-sortable permutations, or even simply to know whether these bases are all finite.

Problem 5.10.

Characterize the basis of the class sortable by an (r,s)(r,s)-stack for general r,s≥2{r,s\geq 2}.

The permutations sortable by a (2,2)(2,2)-stack are counted by A393395,

1,2,6,24,116,628,3636,21956,136428,865700,5583580,36490740,….1,2,6,24,116,628,3636,21956,136428,865700,5583580,36490740,\dots.

Atkinson reported a conjectured expression from the OEIS Superseeker for the generating function of these permutations but did not prove it. Using Combinatorial Exploration [1] and working from the basis in Theorem 5.9, Pantone (personal communication) proved Atkinson’s conjecture, establishing that the generating function for this class has minimal polynomial

2​x​f3−(2​x+3)​f2−(x−7)​f−4.2xf^{3}-(2x+3)f^{2}-(x-7)f-4.

(This differs slightly from Atkinson’s presentation because it includes the constant term 11 for the empty permutation, while Atkinson did not.) It would still be of interest to derive this enumeration directly from the sorting mechanism.

Problem 5.11.

Derive the generating function for the class of (2,2)(2,2)-stack-sortable permutations from the structure of the (2,2)(2,2)-stack.

Given that all known enumerations of (r,s)(r,s)-stack-sortable classes are algebraic, one might ask how far this extends.

Question 5.12.

Does the class of permutations sortable by an (r,s)(r,s)-stack have an algebraic generating function for all r,s≥1r,s\geq 1?

Generalizing 𝒞\mathcal{C}-machines

The (2,2)(2,2)-stack is not a 𝒞\mathcal{C}-machine: it allows popping from either of the top two positions, whereas 𝒞\mathcal{C}-machines pop only from the leftmost position. This suggests a natural generalization of 𝒞\mathcal{C}-machines: allow the pop operation to remove any of the leftmost ss entries from the container, rather than just the leftmost one. Call such a machine an extended 𝒞\mathcal{C}-machine with ss-pop, or a (𝒞,s)(\mathcal{C},s)-machine for short. The 𝒞\mathcal{C}-machines considered earlier are then (𝒞,1)(\mathcal{C},1)-machines, and the (2,2)(2,2)-stack can be viewed as an (Av⁡(123,213),2)(\operatorname{Av}(123,213),2)-machine.

The basis theorem (Theorem 5.6) gives a complete characterization of the classes generated by (𝒞,1)(\mathcal{C},1)-machines. Does a similar result hold more generally?

Problem 5.13.

Is there a basis theorem for (𝒞,s)(\mathcal{C},s)-machines analogous to Theorem 5.6?

Even partial progress would be valuable. For instance, if 𝒞\mathcal{C} is finitely based, does every (𝒞,s)(\mathcal{C},s)-machine generate a class with a finite basis?
